passage: Payal, you keep saying you're tired and don't know why. Let me tell you about your cousin Divyansh. When he was twenty, he'd come home from college and scroll through videos until two in the morning. He said it was relaxing. But he was always irritated and stopped reading, which he used to love. One day he told me the app always seemed to know exactly what would keep him watching. I said, "That's its job." He looked shocked. After that he turned off autoplay, deleted the app from his phone, and only watched on his laptop at set times. He started subscribing to a few long articles he actually wanted to read. He said it felt like getting his mind back.

qa.q: Until what time did Divyansh scroll through videos?
qa.a: He scrolled until two in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh look shocked when told "That's its job"?
qa.a: He realised the app was deliberately designed to keep him watching, which made him feel manipulated.

qa.q: What could Payal try, based on Divyansh's story?
qa.a: Payal could turn off autoplay, limit where and when to watch, and choose what to read on purpose.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's family have seen the change in him?
qa.a: They probably noticed him less irritated and reading again, and felt relieved.

grounding: An elder tells a young adult how a relative resisted manipulative feed design and curated what he consumed.

passage: Noor had three days to finish her thesis chapter, and her phone kept pinging. Every time she opened it to check one message, she ended up scrolling short videos for half an hour. The feed seemed to know she was stressed; it showed her more and more clips about "productivity hacks" and "why you're failing." She felt worse after each one. On the second night, her friend Vijay came over with food. He saw her phone screen. "You're watching videos about working instead of working," he said. Noor laughed, then groaned. She turned off notifications, moved the video app into a folder she'd have to search for, and set a timer for work blocks. She finished the chapter with an hour to spare.

qa.q: How long did Noor have to finish her thesis chapter?
qa.a: She had three days.

qa.q: Why did Noor feel worse after each video?
qa.a: The clips about failing and hacks fed her stress and wasted her time, making her feel more behind.

qa.q: Which of Noor's changes do you think helped most, and why?
qa.a: Turning off notifications removed the constant pull into the feed, so she could stay in her work blocks.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel seeing Noor finish on time?
qa.a: He'd probably feel glad his joke helped her notice the trap.

grounding: It shows a young woman under time pressure resisting an engagement-driven feed and taking control of her attention.

passage: In their shared flat in Hyderabad, Imran noticed his flatmate Vidya had started unfollowing accounts every evening. "What are you doing?" he asked. "Cleaning my feed," she said. "It kept showing me angry news and people with perfect lives. I felt awful after scrolling." She showed him how she'd followed a few science pages, a cooking channel and a friend's art account instead. "Now when I open it, it's mostly stuff I actually want." Imran laughed. "The app will still try to pull you back." "I know. That's why I also set a daily limit." Imran checked his own screen time that night: five hours. He didn't say anything to Vidya. But the next morning, he unfollowed ten accounts.

qa.q: How many accounts did Imran unfollow the next morning?
qa.a: He unfollowed ten accounts.

qa.q: Why did Vidya decide to clean her feed?
qa.a: The feed kept showing angry news and perfect lives, which left her feeling awful after scrolling.

qa.q: What made Vidya's approach to her feed effective?
qa.a: She chose what to follow on purpose and set a daily limit, knowing the app would still try to pull her back.

qa.q: Why might Imran not have said anything to Vidya?
qa.a: He may have felt a little embarrassed by his five hours of screen time and preferred to change quietly.

grounding: It shows young adults consciously curating their feeds and resisting engagement-maximising design.

passage:
'Seema, dinner's been on the table ten minutes.'
'Coming, Jomon, one second.'
'You said that at eight.'
She finally sat down, still scrolling. 'It's weird. I opened the video app to check one recipe. Now it's showing me people fighting in airports.'
'That's how it works, chechi. It keeps giving you whatever makes you stay.'
'I know. I still stay.' She put the phone face down. 'I watched one angry clip and then the whole feed turned angry. I felt terrible afterwards.'
Amma, ladling sambar: 'So why not delete it?'
'I use it for cooking and my coding tutorials.' Seema thought. 'Maybe I turn off autoplay. Unfollow the rage stuff. Tap not interested.'
Jomon grinned. 'And set a timer.'
'Twenty minutes. You check on me.'
'Deal. Now eat before it's cold.'

qa.q: Why did Seema first open the video app?
qa.a: To check one recipe.

qa.q: How did Seema feel after the feed turned angry?
qa.a: She felt terrible, and her line 'I still stay' shows frustration at how the feed keeps hold of her.

qa.q: Which of Seema's ideas help her take back control?
qa.a: Turning off autoplay, unfollowing or marking rage content as not interesting, and a twenty-minute timer with her brother checking let her keep the useful parts.

qa.q: How does Jomon see the feed?
qa.a: He sees it as built to keep showing whatever makes you stay, so he suggests a timer and teases her gently instead of blaming her.

grounding: A family dinner conversation shows a young woman noticing a manipulative feed and deciding how to curate it.

passage: Last year I realised I didn't choose most of what went into my head. I'd open a news app for the cricket score and forty minutes later I'd be furious about a stranger's comment. Leela, my lab partner, once asked, 'Chetan, what did you read this week that you actually remember?' I couldn't answer. That stung. So I tried an experiment. I turned off every notification except messages from people. I made a short list of sources I trusted, two newsletters and one long-form magazine site, and read them on Sunday mornings with tea. Whenever the feed pushed something at me, I asked: did I go looking for this? Some weeks I slid right back. But I remember more now, and my interests feel like mine again, not something a machine handed me.

qa.q: What did Chetan read on Sunday mornings?
qa.a: Two newsletters and one long-form magazine site from a short list of trusted sources, with tea.

qa.q: Why did Leela's question sting Chetan?
qa.a: Chetan could not name anything remembered from a whole week of reading, which showed how little of it had really been chosen.

qa.q: What question helped Chetan resist the feed?
qa.a: Asking 'did I go looking for this?' made Chetan notice when content was pushed rather than chosen.

qa.q: If Leela had not asked that question, what might have changed?
qa.a: Chetan might have kept scrolling without noticing, angry and scattered, with nothing to prompt a different approach.

grounding: A student reflects on resisting engagement-driven feeds by turning off notifications and choosing their own sources.

passage: Internship supervisor's note, week 4. Tushar asked to talk after missing a second deadline. He showed me his screen-time page himself: five hours a day on a short-video app, most of it after 11 p.m. "I open it for one video and it's two hours later," he said. "It knows exactly what I'll watch next." He had already spotted the tricks: endless scroll, autoplay, the red dot that never quite goes away. Hemant, his co-intern, shared how he had moved the app off his home screen and now follows only three cooking channels he genuinely enjoys. Tushar decided to turn off notifications and autoplay, and to read a weekly news digest instead of the feed. I've suggested we review his deadlines together on Fridays for a month. — Ms Qureshi, team lead

qa.q: How many hours a day did Tushar's screen-time page show?
qa.a: Five hours a day.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he said the app knows exactly what he'll watch next?
qa.a: Tushar seemed frustrated and uneasy, feeling that the app was steering his time rather than him.

qa.q: Which of Tushar's changes target the app's design most directly?
qa.a: Turning off notifications and autoplay removes the red dot and the automatic next video, and a weekly digest replaces the endless feed.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel sharing his own method?
qa.a: Hemant probably felt glad and a little proud to help, having found a calmer way to use the same kind of app.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows an intern recognising manipulative feed design and choosing what he takes in.

passage:
Sunday, late
Did an experiment today. Scrolled my feed for ten minutes and wrote down every video. Seven out of twelve were skincare routines or "glow-ups". I searched for ONE moisturiser in June and now apparently that's my whole personality. By the end I felt worse about my face than when I started 😔
Nilesh says the feed isn't showing me what I like, it's showing me what keeps me there. Creepy, but it makes sense.
So: I pressed "not interested" on every skincare video, unfollowed four accounts that make me feel ugly, and followed the city library, two birdwatchers and a woman who restores old chairs. I also moved the app into a folder called "later".
Tomorrow I'll check whether the feed changed. Even if it hasn't, I decide what I open.
— Ritu

qa.q: How many of the twelve videos were skincare routines or glow-ups?
qa.a: Seven out of twelve.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel at the end of the ten-minute scroll?
qa.a: Ritu felt insecure about appearance, and a bit annoyed at being pushed so much skincare content.

qa.q: Which of Ritu's steps are most likely to change what Ritu takes in?
qa.a: Pressing 'not interested', unfollowing accounts that bring Ritu down, following things Ritu values and hiding the app in a folder all reshape what shows up and how often.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Ritu's experiment?
qa.a: Nilesh would likely feel pleased that the idea about the feed helped, and curious to see whether it changes.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult testing a feed, seeing how it hooks attention, and curating what to follow.

passage:
In the small town, Urmila had started watching short videos after work to relax. The feed kept showing her angrier and angrier clips: people fighting, shouting about politics, scary news.
She felt tense and couldn't sleep. But she kept scrolling.
Her friend Pradeep, who ran the cyber café, said, "The app shows you what keeps you watching. Anger keeps people watching."
"So it's not showing me the world?"
"It's showing you what works on you."
Urmila went home and pressed "not interested" on the angry videos. She followed a few cooking and farming channels and turned off autoplay.
A week later she said, "My feed is boring now. I sleep better."

qa.q: Who ran the cyber café?
qa.a: Pradeep.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling while watching the angry videos?
qa.a: Urmila felt tense and anxious, unable to sleep.

qa.q: What steps did Urmila take to curate her feed?
qa.a: She marked angry videos "not interested," followed calmer channels and turned off autoplay.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see the recommendation feed?
qa.a: Pradeep sees it as designed to show whatever keeps people watching, even anger.

grounding: A young woman in a small town learns how feeds push anger and curates her intake.

passage:
In Madrid, Omar noticed he opened the video app first thing in the morning, before he even got up. Two hours would pass.
His friend Lucia said, "Look at what it shows you."
He scrolled: clips of luxury cars, gym bodies, people getting rich fast.
"I don't even care about cars," Omar said.
"It learnt you'd watch them. It's designed to keep you there."
Omar decided to curate. He unfollowed accounts that made him feel bad. He subscribed to two news podcasts and a language channel. He moved the app off his home screen.
Two weeks later he told Lucia, "I'm learning Arabic properly now. And I'm less jealous of strangers."

qa.q: What did Omar's feed show?
qa.a: Clips of luxury cars, gym bodies, people getting rich fast.

qa.q: What was Omar feeling about the feed's content?
qa.a: Omar felt uneasy and jealous, though he didn't even care about cars.

qa.q: What changes helped Omar control his information intake?
qa.a: Unfollowing accounts that made him feel bad, choosing podcasts and a language channel, and moving the app off the home screen.

qa.q: How does Lucia see the video app?
qa.a: Lucia sees it as designed to keep users hooked by showing whatever they'll watch.

grounding: A young man in Spain notices manipulative feed design and curates his information intake.

passage:
In the Bengaluru office, Anand's lunch breaks disappeared into his phone. He'd check a news app and an hour would vanish in headlines about disasters and celebrity fights.
His colleague Rehana watched him one day. "You look stressed after lunch."
"There's so much happening."
"Or the app is showing you the most clickable things."
Anand realised he couldn't remember a single useful thing he'd read that week.
He deleted the news app. Instead, he subscribed to one weekly newsletter and read it on Sunday with coffee. Lunches became walks with Rehana.
"I know less gossip," he said. "But I understand more."

qa.q: What did Anand subscribe to instead of the news app?
qa.a: One weekly newsletter.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling after lunch before the change?
qa.a: Anand felt stressed and scattered after endless headlines.

qa.q: What choice helped Anand resist the attention trap?
qa.a: He deleted the app and chose a weekly newsletter read at a set time.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel about the lunchtime walks?
qa.a: Rehana probably enjoys the company and is glad Anand is less stressed.

grounding: A young office worker recognises an attention trap and chooses a calmer way to follow news.

passage:
Hi Suraj,
You asked why I've been quieter online. I'm writing it down so it makes sense.
In March I noticed I opened the video app to check one thing and came out an hour later, angry about strangers I'd never meet. The feed kept giving me fights: people yelling about politics, about food, about anything. The angrier I got, the more it gave.
So I did an experiment. I unfollowed forty accounts that made me furious. I turned off autoplay and all notifications except messages. I subscribed to two long weekly newsletters, one on science and one on books, and read them on Sunday with coffee.
First week felt empty. Second week, calmer. Third week, I'd read a whole novel.
I still watch dumb cat videos. But now I choose, instead of the feed choosing for me.
Try it for a week? Tell me what you notice.
Maria

qa.q: How many accounts did Maria unfollow?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: How did Maria feel after an hour on the feed?
qa.a: Maria felt angry, stirred up about strangers Maria would never meet.

qa.q: Why did Maria's changes work against the feed's design?
qa.a: Turning off autoplay and notifications and choosing slow sources removed the hooks built to keep Maria engaged, so Maria picked what to read.

qa.q: How might Suraj respond to Maria's invitation?
qa.a: Suraj might feel curious but doubtful, and trying it for a week could show how much the feed shapes Suraj's mood.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult resisting engagement-maximising design by deliberately curating information intake.

passage:
Chandrika, you asked on your show how I noticed the feed was shaping me. I'm Gargi, and it was a Sunday lunch.
My uncle said something mild about a news story, and I exploded. I quoted five things I'd seen that week. When my cousin asked where they came from, I couldn't say. They were clips, reposts, angry voices, all pushed to me after I'd watched one video in January.
That night I scrolled back through my history. It was the same kind of video, again and again, each one more extreme. I hadn't searched for any of them.
So I cleaned house. I cleared my watch history, muted trending topics, and chose three news sources I could check. I follow a few people who disagree with me politely.
I still have opinions. But now I can tell you where they came from.

qa.q: When had Gargi watched the one video that started the pattern?
qa.a: In January.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling during the outburst at lunch?
qa.a: Gargi felt angry and certain, and later shaken to realise Gargi couldn't say where those facts came from.

qa.q: Which of Gargi's steps give the best protection from manipulative design?
qa.a: Clearing the watch history, muting trending topics and choosing a few checkable sources, because they stop the feed escalating what Gargi sees.

qa.q: How might Gargi's uncle have experienced the Sunday outburst?
qa.a: The uncle may have felt shocked and hurt that a mild comment set off such anger.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing how a recommendation feed escalated personal views and consciously curating sources.

passage:
I'm Madhav. I share a flat with Gargi, and I watched her change over one semester.
At the start, her phone was always in her hand. She'd lie on the sofa scrolling short videos with the sound on, laughing, then going quiet, then scrolling again. At dinner she'd check it between bites. She said she was "resting".
In October she stuck a note on the fridge: "What did I choose to see today?" She moved the video app off her home screen and put a book app in its place. She started saying things like, "The feed wants me angry tonight. No thanks," and closing it.
I don't know exactly what she felt. Some days she still scrolled for hours. But by December, she was the one telling me to stop doom-scrolling. That's how I knew something had shifted.

qa.q: What did Gargi write on the note on the fridge?
qa.a: "What did I choose to see today?"

qa.q: What does Gargi saying "The feed wants me angry tonight" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Gargi felt more aware and determined, noticing how the feed tries to stir her up and choosing to resist.

qa.q: How could Madhav support Gargi's new habits?
qa.a: Madhav could keep phones off at dinner too and join her in choosing what they watch together.

qa.q: Why is Madhav careful about saying what Gargi felt?
qa.a: Madhav only sees her actions from outside and can't be sure of her inner state, so Madhav describes what changed.

grounding: Illustrates, through a flatmate's eyes, a young adult resisting engagement-maximising design and curating what she sees.

Friday: Vandana opened the short-video app "for five minutes" after dinner and looked up at 1:20 a.m. The feed had learned she liked cooking clips, then angry arguments about cooking, then more arguments. She felt oddly angry and couldn't say why.
The next Wednesday: Her classmate Sabina showed her the settings page during a free period. "See? Autoplay, endless scroll, notifications. It's built to keep you going." Vandana turned off autoplay and all notifications, and unfollowed the three accounts that made her angriest. She felt a small, stubborn satisfaction.
Two weeks later, Sunday: She still used the app, but by choice, searching for one recipe and closing it. She had also started a list of five blogs she actually wanted to read. The late nights were rarer. She cooked the dal from the recipe and sent Sabina a photo: "Made it. Didn't watch 40 videos first 🎉"

qa.q: What changes helped Vandana take back control of her feed?
